skill.name: networkx
skill.description: Guidance for building, analyzing, visualizing, and exchanging graph data with NetworkX in Python.
skill.summary: Build, analyze, visualize, and export graph networks with NetworkX.
skill.author: davila7

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives caused by Markdown code fences, NetworkX graph terminology, documentation links, and local file I/O examples. No prompt injection, data exfiltration, or hidden command execution was found. One medium documentation risk remains because pickle deserialization examples lack trusted-input warnings.

remediation.issue: Pickle loading examples do not warn about untrusted files.
remediation.suggestion: Add a warning before pickle.load and nx.read_gpickle that pickle files must come from trusted sources; recommend GraphML or JSON for untrusted exchange.

remediation.issue: File export examples use fixed demonstration filenames.
remediation.suggestion: Clarify that generated files should be written only to user-approved paths inside the active project.

remediation.issue: Optional dependency installation guidance may trigger environment changes.
remediation.suggestion: State that agents should ask for user confirmation before installing NetworkX optional dependencies.

semantic_findings.title: Unsafe Pickle Deserialization Guidance
semantic_findings.description: The I/O reference shows pickle.load and nx.read_gpickle examples without a warning about untrusted files. Loading attacker-controlled pickle data can execute arbitrary Python code.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The referenced lines directly show pickle deserialization paths. The risk depends on whether files are trusted, but the documentation lacks that safety boundary.

content.value_statement: Graph data is hard to model, inspect, and explain. This skill guides NetworkX workflows for building, analyzing, visualizing, and exporting networks.
actual_capabilities: Create NetworkX graph, directed graph, multigraph, and multidigraph structures with node and edge attributes.
Compute shortest paths, centrality, clustering, connectivity, communities, matching, and traversal metrics.
Generate random, lattice, tree, bipartite, and social network model graphs.
Read and write edge lists, GraphML, GML, JSON, CSV, matrix, database, and DOT formats.
Create static and interactive network visualizations with layout and styling guidance.
Suggest performance approaches for large sparse graphs and approximate algorithms.
limitations: It provides guidance and examples; it does not install NetworkX or execute analysis by itself.
Large graphs may need specialized backends, memory planning, or approximate algorithms.
Interactive visualizations require optional libraries such as Plotly or PyVis.
Pickle examples should only be used with trusted graph files.

use_cases.title: Analyze Relationship Data
use_cases.description: Build graphs from entity relationships, calculate centrality, and identify important nodes or communities.

use_cases.title: Model Research Networks
use_cases.description: Explore citation, biological, transportation, or social networks with standard algorithms and reproducible layouts.

use_cases.title: Export Network Pipelines
use_cases.description: Choose file formats and integration patterns for moving graph data between Python tools and visualization systems.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Basic Graph
prompt_templates.prompt: Use NetworkX to model my entities and relationships. Explain which graph type fits and list the node and edge attributes to include.

prompt_templates.title: Analyze Network Metrics
prompt_templates.prompt: Given my graph goal and data columns, recommend NetworkX metrics for centrality, paths, clustering, and connectivity. Explain what each metric means.

prompt_templates.title: Visualize and Export Results
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a NetworkX workflow that loads my edge data, creates a clear visualization, and exports analysis results in suitable formats.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Scalable Graph Workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my large graph analysis plan. Recommend memory-aware data structures, approximate algorithms, safe file formats, and validation checks.

output_examples.input: I have a CSV with source, target, and weight columns for customer referrals.
output_examples.output: Recommended workflow: load the table, build a weighted graph, inspect connected components, rank nodes by centrality, and export a summary table.

output_examples.input: I need to find groups in a citation network and explain the most influential papers.
output: Use community detection to group related papers.
Use PageRank and betweenness centrality to compare influence.
Visualize communities with consistent colors and a reproducible layout seed.

output_examples.input: My graph is too large for exact betweenness centrality.
output_examples.output: Use approximate centrality, filter to relevant subgraphs, store sparse structures, and document the sampling settings for repeatable results.

best_practices: Set random seeds for generated graphs and force-directed layouts to keep results reproducible.
Choose the graph type before analysis so directed edges, parallel edges, and attributes are handled correctly.
Use transparent exchange formats for untrusted data, and reserve pickle files for trusted internal workflows.
anti_patterns: Loading pickle graph files from untrusted sources.
Running exact centrality algorithms on very large graphs without sampling or performance checks.
Visualizing dense networks without filtering, layout planning, or readable labels.

faq.question: What is NetworkX best for?
faq.answer: NetworkX is best for Python graph modeling, algorithm exploration, network metrics, and clear analysis workflows.

faq.question: Can it handle directed or multigraph data?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill explains Graph, DiGraph, MultiGraph, and MultiDiGraph choices for different relationship structures.

faq.question: Does this skill create visualizations?
faq.answer: It provides guidance for NetworkX drawing, matplotlib styling, layouts, and optional interactive visualization libraries.

faq.question: Which file formats does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers edge lists, adjacency lists, GraphML, GML, JSON, CSV, pandas, matrices, SQL, DOT, and Cytoscape formats.

faq.question: Is it safe to use pickle with graph data?
faq.answer: Only use pickle with trusted files. Prefer GraphML, JSON, or CSV when exchanging graph data with other users or systems.

faq.question: Can Claude, Codex, and Claude Code use it?
faq.answer: Yes. The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code workflows.
